title: Rep. Chuck Edwards withdraws from re-election after ethics censure recommendation
dek: Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) announced on August 5, 2026, that he is withdrawing from his re-election campaign following a House Ethics Committee recommendation to censure him over allegations of inappropriate conduct toward two female staffers. Edwards denies the allegations were sexual in nature and said he cooperated with the investigation.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Edwards announced his withdrawal from re-election three days after the House Ethics Committee recommended censure, finding he engaged in a pattern of unprofessional conduct including lavish gifts, comments on appearance, and invitations to intimate dinners and vacations toward two young female staffers.
bottom_line: Edwards will complete his current term but exit Congress after the 2026 cycle, sparing the House a full censure vote that was likely to proceed. The withdrawal settles the immediate ethics matter but leaves open whether the full chamber would have voted to approve the committee's recommendation and what that precedent might signal for future ethics cases.
body: Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) announced on Wednesday, August 5, 2026, that he will not seek re-election, three days after the House Ethics Committee recommended censuring him over allegations of inappropriate conduct toward two female staffers. In a post on X, the 65-year-old congressman stated, "After much prayer and reflection, I've decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign. I will complete my current term."

Edwards' announcement came after the bipartisan Ethics Committee released a 25-page report on Monday recommending censure. The committee found that Edwards "engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers" and "violated the House Code of Official Conduct by failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers."

According to the committee's findings, Edwards' pattern of behavior included providing young women with lavish and recurring gifts, making comments regarding their appearance and dress, inviting them to intimate dinners and vacations, sending notes expressing effusive affection, and inviting them to other activities as a way to spend time together. The committee concluded this conduct "would lead a reasonable observer to interpret it as" sexual harassment.

The Ethics Committee said it found no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with or propositioned any of his staffers, and concluded that the allegations "do not implicate quid pro quo sexual harassment" or violate "the 'letter' of federal sexual harassment law." The panel also noted that Edwards denied his actions were intended to be sexual or romantic in nature and that he cooperated with the investigation.

Edwards previously called the allegations "baseless" and welcomed an investigation in a May statement to NBC News. His counsel submitted a 15-page rebuttal to the committee's findings characterizing them as "unfounded."

Edwards is a former state lawmaker who ousted Rep. Madison Cawthorn in the GOP primary in 2022. His withdrawal from re-election removes him from competition in a competitive Western North Carolina district. The full House has not yet voted on the Ethics Committee's censure recommendation.
